findings.quote: The Real Gluten-Free Guide to Korea: A Couple's Field-Tested Handbook (2026)
findings.why: At ~76 characters before layout.js appends ' | Gluten-Free Korea' (~96 total), the title will be truncated in SERPs, and the truncated remainder still contains neither 'celiac' nor 'travel' from the target keyword.
findings.fix: Retitle to something like 'Celiac Travel in Korea: A Field-Tested Guide' (43 chars, 63 with the suffix) and let the 'couple's handbook' framing live in the description or H1 subhead.

findings.quote: Imported Japanese tamari is the easiest GF substitute in Seoul (Lotte Mart, larger Emart, Kim's Club).
findings.why: If this FAQ is emitted as structured data, the rich result asserts specific retail availability that the article body never establishes — the body mentions tamari only once, as 'GF tamari in the bag'. The BBQ answer has the same problem with '양념 안 한 고기 있나요?' and salt-grilled samgyeopsal, neither of which appears in the body's phrase or restaurant sections.
findings.fix: Add two or three sentences in the label/shopping section naming where you have actually bought tamari and when, and give Korean BBQ a short in-body subsection covering the unseasoned-meat phrase and salt-grilled samgyeopsal, so every FAQ answer is visibly supported.

findings.quote: The only GFCO-certified gluten-free pizza in Korea, as far as we've been able to confirm.
findings.why: The strongest trust claim in the piece — third-party certification — rests entirely on the author's say-so. The same applies to the regulatory claim about the mandated allergen list. No external source is linked or dated anywhere in the article.
findings.fix: Link the GFCO certified-product directory entry with the date you checked it, and link the MFDS allergen-labelling notice (with its revision date) beside the allergen-line explanation.

findings.quote: lists the major 22 flagged allergens for that product
findings.why: Factual accuracy is the other judge's axis, but the count of Korea's mandatory allergen-labelling items is commonly cited as 19, not 22, and an unsourced precise number weakens an otherwise checkable section.
findings.fix: Verify the current count against the MFDS labelling standard and cite it with the effective date, or drop the number and say 'the mandated allergen list'.

findings.quote: The rest of this series, as each post lands:

criteria.note: The reader gets exact Korean phrases, a reconfirmation script, specific words to scan on packaging, a checkable certification name, branch-level confirmation advice, and a correction channel.

findings.quote: Plain salt-grilled samgyeopsal is reliably safe.
findings.why: This is an absolute safety verdict delivered about the single highest cross-contamination setting in Korean dining: a grill and tongs shared with soy-marinated meat, communal banchan, and a ssamjang bowl. The answer sits in the frontmatter FAQ, so it can surface on its own, detached from the NCGS caveat in the body. A celiac reader acting on it eats gluten.
findings.fix: Replace with a conditional: "Plain salt-grilled samgyeopsal is the safest order, but for celiacs ask for a fresh grill plate and clean tongs, skip ssamjang and sauced banchan, and treat a grill previously used for marinated meat as contaminated."

findings.quote: search for 밀 in the allergen line, return or keep. That's the entire operation.
findings.why: Korea's mandatory allergen labelling covers wheat only. Barley (보리) and rye (호밀) are not mandatory allergen declarations, so they routinely will not appear in the 알레르기 유발물질 line even when present as ingredients. Presenting an allergen-line scan for 밀 as the complete check will pass barley-malt and barley-containing products as clean for a celiac reader.
findings.fix: State plainly that Korea's mandatory allergen line covers wheat only, that 보리 and 호밀 must be hunted in the full ingredient list rather than the allergen line, and that celiac readers cannot stop at the allergen declaration.

findings.why: Package-colour and flavour-level verdicts across a snack list are claims a celiac reader will act on in a store aisle, yet none is tied to a label photo, an ingredient quotation, a manufacturer confirmation, or a date checked. The blanket "re-verify on the actual packet" hedge does not make the individual verdicts checkable.
findings.fix: For each snack, add the date the label was read and the specific ingredient-line wording observed, or move the list to a separately maintained page with per-item check dates.

findings.quote: I called the franchise headquarters directly to confirm
findings.why: Korean manufacturers and franchises reformulate without notice. An undated phone confirmation reads as current to a reader four months after publication, with no way to judge whether the answer still holds.
findings.fix: Add the month the call was made and a line noting that franchise recipes change, so readers should re-confirm with HQ or the branch before ordering.

findings.quote: A brunch spot with oatmeal pancakes and sandwiches that can be modified with GF bread swaps.
findings.why: A bread swap in a shared non-dedicated brunch kitchen carries board, toaster and prep-surface contamination risk that the entry never raises, and oats add a further celiac-specific caveat. The generic "still ask every visit" line does not cover the mechanism.
findings.fix: Add a Tier 2 cross-contamination note: swapped GF bread in a shared kitchen is a low-gluten, not gluten-free, outcome, and celiac readers should ask about a separate toaster and prep surface.
